items.title: ASSESSING THE ACCEPTANCE OF CHATGPT AMONG HIGHER EDUCATION STUDENTS: A CASE STUDY IN PAHANG
items.abstract: The current study, which is entitled Evaluating the Assessing the Acceptance of ChatGPT Among Higher Education Students: A Case Study in Pahang, aimed to assess the behavioural intention of university students with regard to using ChatGPT in various academic levels. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) was selected as a cross-sectional survey approach, data were collected from 184 respondents between March and May 2025 through both online and printed questionnaires. The core antecedents included in the analysis were the performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and personal innovativeness and were operationalised using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive analysis revealed an overall mean behavioural intention score of 3.523 (SD = 0.901), indicating a generally positive inclination toward ChatGPT adoption. Notably, both bachelor and postgraduate students erred higher mean scores (4.400 and 4.370, respectively) in comparison with students of the foundation level (3.393), which suggests that students of higher learning level assign AI-based technologies a higher academic rating. These results highlight an increasing openness to generative AI among the population of higher education, and at the same time, they indicate the presence of strong inequalities among the academic layers. Therefore, the findings reinforce the need to introduce specific AI-literacy programmes and responsible digital education to facilitate fair and responsible usage. Despite the methodological constraints, such as sampling, and the disproportional number of groups, the generalisability of the findings is diluted but still, the study provides useful information to the growing discourse on AI implementation into higher education, at least in the developing regional milieus. Moreover, the study presents practical research implications to institutions of higher education working to come up with evidence-based, inclusionary, and ethically sustainable strategies to implement ChatGPT and other similar technologies in pedagogical and curricular contexts.

items.title: Assessment of teacher performance and learner behavior using artificial intelligence in higher education: an integrative review of literature
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming quality assurance in higher education by enabling adaptive, data-driven assessments of teaching performance and student learning. This integrative review synthesizes the purposes, methodologies, and outcomes of AI-enabled assessments, examines emerging technological trends, and identifies opportunities for improving teaching quality and learner support. Methods An integrative review was conducted using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, with study identification and selection reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Of 367 records identified, 21 studies were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Descriptive and thematic analyses were supplemented by keyword network mapping using VOSviewer version 1.6.20. Results Most studies were multi-authored (71.43%) and published in interdisciplinary education and technology journals (57.14%), with publication activity concentrated in 2024 (28.57%) and 2025 (33.33%). The Western Pacific Region accounted for the largest proportion of studies (38.10%), while no studies originated from the African Region. Teacher performance was the predominant assessment focus ( n = 11; 52.38%), followed by learner behavior ( n = 4; 19.05%) and learner performance ( n = 3; 14.29%). Teacher-focused assessments primarily analyzed learner-generated data using machine learning and natural language processing, whereas some learner-focused assessments employed video-based data and computer vision. Machine learning and natural language processing were the most frequently identified technological approaches ( n = 6), followed by computer vision and multimodal or speech recognition approaches ( n = 3). Most implementations followed a data-input, AI-processing, and output-generation structure, with varying levels of complexity. Thematic analysis identified four domains, while keyword network analysis revealed eight clusters. Discussion The findings highlight a fragmented assessment landscape in which teacher performance and learner behavior are predominantly examined independently. Although learner behavior may provide complementary evidence of teaching effectiveness, reciprocal relationships between teaching and learning remain insufficiently explored. Geographic disparities and methodological heterogeneity further constrain the generalizability and institutional applicability of existing evidence. Conclusion AI offers promising opportunities to strengthen teaching evaluation and learner support in higher education. However, broader geographic representation, methodological rigor, validated assessment frameworks, and equitable, human-supervised implementation are essential to ensure that institutional adoption is guided by robust evidence. Systematic Review Registration https://osf.io/ugt4w .

items.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

items.abstract: Résumé. Le generative engine optimization (GEO) désigne le travail qui vise à faire citer une marque, avec des informations exactes, dans les réponses rédigées par les IA génératives. Cette note décrit la méthode d’audit et d’accompagnement de NEXUS GEO, telle qu’elle est publiée sur son site. L’audit évalue un site et sa présence en ligne selon le Référentiel GEO-47 : 8 piliers, 47 critères, un score global sur 100. Sa grille vaut pour toutes les IA ; la mesure de la présence de la marque porte sur cinq IA (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral et Google AI Overviews), face à trois concurrents nommés. La note présente les trois étapes de la méthode, les indicateurs, les livrables, ce qui est publié et ce qui ne l’est pas, et les limites de la démarche. Abstract. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of getting a brand cited, with accurate information, in answers written by generative AI assistants. This note describes the audit and support method of NEXUS GEO, a French agency, as published on its website. The audit assesses a website and its online presence against the GEO-47 Framework: 8 pillars, 47 criteria and an overall score out of 100. The assessment grid applies to all AI assistants; the brand’s presence is measured on five of them (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral and Google AI Overviews), against three named competitors. The note sets out the three stages of the method, its indicators and deliverables, what is published and what is not, and the method’s limits. items.title: Authenticity and Trust in AI-Mediated Digital Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes user experiences across digital environments, yet research explaining how AI simultaneously builds and undermines trust remains fragmented. This conceptual chapter introduces the Authenticity Paradox, proposing that AI-enabled personalisation initially enhances perceived authenticity, fostering trust and continued engagement. However, as users become aware of the hidden algorithmic processes underlying personalised interactions, they may reinterpret earlier experiences as engineered rather than genuine, leading to reduced perceived authenticity and declining trust. Drawing on literature from ride-hailing platforms, virtual influencers, and professional AI environments, the chapter develops an integrative conceptual framework demonstrating a common relational mechanism while highlighting context-specific vulnerabilities. The chapter concludes with implications for responsible AI design, transparency, explainability, and future research on trustworthy AI across AI-mediated environments.

items.title: Author-Informed Stance Detection: A Dataset and Findings
items.abstract: Stance detection in social media is challenging, as interpreting a text often requires understanding the author's perspective. We re-frame political stance detection as an author-informed text understanding task, where it is desired to infer both the author's political leaning and their stance towards the target from the text. We first show that human annotators struggle to infer authors' political leanings and stances from individual tweets, and that pretrained large language models (LLMs) perform below human level in this setting. We then demonstrate that author context improves stance detection for both humans and LLMs, with particularly pronounced benefits for tweets perceived as sarcastic. Through extensive experiments, we further show that LLMs can be effectively fine-tuned to predict authors' political affiliations, and that author-informed fine-tuning yields better stance detection performance than standard fine-tuning. This approach not only surpasses human performance but also improves generalization across datasets. To support further research on author-informed political stance detection, we release a large dataset of stance-labeled tweets enriched with author-context information.

items.title: Automated deep learning tool for robust colony counting in vaccine immunogenicity bioassays
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The microcolony multiplex opsonophagocytic killing assay (mMOPA) is a critical functional assay for evaluating pneumococcal vaccine immunogenicity; however, its colony-counting readout is scientist-dependent and time‑consuming. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In this study, we developed and optimized a deep learning model (DLM) colony-counting tool by adapting the Segment Anything (SAM) foundation model and evaluated its performance using historical assay qualification datasets spanning 12 pneumococcal serotypes, with additional benchmarking against blinded human expert counts. RESULTS: The DLM-derived counts demonstrated strong correlation and agreement with both historical CTL ImmunoSpot® counts and expert counts. Notably, DLM outperformed CTL for a challenging serotype and produced comparable opsonophagocytic titers with those generated using CTL counts within the representative samples evaluated. These results establish the DLM approach as fit for purpose for mMOPA readouts. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work removes a key throughput bottleneck in mMOPA, enables a "walkaway" colony-counting workflow supporting improved operational efficiency and scalability for large clinical studies, and highlights the broader value of integrating bioanalytical expertise with modern computer vision to advance scalable, image-based bioassays in vaccine and drug development.

items.title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
items.abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. items.title: Automation Bias and Deskilling in Radiology AI: A Confidence-stratified Triage Model for Workflow Integration
items.abstract: Radiology is adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than it is studying what AI does to radiologists' perceptual expertise and interpretive skill. The question has partly shifted from whether these tools perform well on benchmark tasks to what happens to clinical judgment when use of these tools becomes routine. Two risks accompany this transition: automation bias, the tendency to follow AI suggestions without adequate scrutiny, and deskilling, the erosion of perceptual and interpretive ability through disuse, typically revealed when AI support is withdrawn. Incorrect AI output degrades accuracy regardless of experience, the benefit of assistance varies unpredictably across readers and tasks, and performance falls after AI withdrawal; neither risk has been studied longitudinally in radiology. A confidence-stratified triage model is proposed in which calibrated AI confidence, not findings alone, routes cases to low-, intermediate-, or high-confidence streams: output withheld until independent reading, shown with uncertainty signals and a checklist, or shown with random blinded audit. Demonstrated local confidence calibration is a precondition for deployment, and stream thresholds and audit rates should be weighted by task and potential clinical harm, not error probability alone. Rather than applying one workflow to every case, the model redistributes radiologist attention to where AI error is most likely and most consequential, operationalizing four principles: keeping the radiologist in the decision loop, making AI uncertainty visible, inserting targeted cognitive friction, and governing the human-AI interaction as a system. A research agenda to determine whether these countermeasures reduce automation bias and skill erosion in practice is also proposed.

items.title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
items.abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

items.title: Awareness and Readiness of Pre-Service Special Educators for Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Inclusive Education
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education offers transformative opportunities, particularly for inclusive classrooms where students with diverse needs require adaptive and supportive technologies. Despite this advancement, there is limited understanding of how prepared pre-service special educators are to use AI tools effectively. This study addresses this gap by examining the awareness, readiness, and AI-related competencies of pre-service special educators in India. The research specifically investigates their awareness, readiness and technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) and explores differences based on demographic factors such as gender, level of professional training (B.Ed. vs M.Ed.), and prior exposure to AI. A descriptive and inferential quantitative research design was adopted, utilizing a structured questionnaire administered to 200 pre-service special educators. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, and correlation to identify trends and associations. Findings revealed moderate levels of awareness and readiness, with significant differences linked to demographic variables and prior training. Notably, higher TPACK scores were strongly associated with greater readiness to adopt AI. These results have practical implications for teacher education programs, suggesting the need for targeted AI training and curriculum enhancements to equip future special educators for inclusive, technology-rich learning environments.

items.title: Barriers and Facilitators to Peer Support Among the Healthcare Workforce: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Healthcare professionals work within complex and demanding environments characterised by substantial responsibility, emotional demands, high workloads, exposure to distressing and potentially traumatic events, and persistent workforce pressures (Hansel et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2018; Sattar et al., 2024). These occupational demands can affect healthcare workers’ psychological and emotional wellbeing and highlight the importance of accessible and appropriate support mechanisms within healthcare settings. Despite increasing recognition of healthcare worker wellbeing as an important workforce and organisational priority, healthcare professionals may be reluctant to access formal psychological or mental health services (Gold et al., 2016; Trusty et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Young et al., 2025). Peer support represents one alternative or complementary approach. Existing evidence suggests that peer support may help reduce feelings of isolation, strengthen resilience, and support emotional wellbeing and adaptive coping among healthcare professionals (Walker & Peterson, 2021; Watson, 2019). However, peer-support initiatives vary considerably in their purpose, structure, mode of delivery, target populations, level of formality, and organisational context. Consequently, there is a need to systematically map the existing evidence. This scoping review aims to map the existing literature on peer support among healthcare professionals, care staff, and non-clinical healthcare staff, with particular attention to the characteristics of peer-support approaches and the barriers and facilitators influencing their implementation, access, uptake, and engagement. The review will also identify gaps in the current evidence and areas requiring further research.

items.title: Barriers and the Invisible Hurdles
items.abstract: Abstract The silent cry for help is often a voice that is faint and hesitant, particularly for Black males in community colleges. Stigmas tied to their identity and cultural challenges that arise before they even arrive on campus contribute to the difficulties they face. This chapter explores the unique challenges confronting Black male students, highlighting barriers created by traditional educational structures and the lack of culturally responsive approaches. It underscores how eurocentric curricula and teacher-centered methods fail to meet the need for autonomy, competence, and relatedness creating gaps in connecting, communicating, and discovering. Emphasizing self-determination, the chapter illustrates how intrinsic motivation, and tailored support can empower Black males. It also discusses the role of mentoring and coaching, as well as alternative learning environments that align with the cultural and social contexts. Overall, it calls for a reimagining of higher education to create inclusive and equitable spaces for Black male students.

items.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
items.abstract: Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.

items.title: Behavioral Biases in AI-Driven Pricing and Revenue Optimization
items.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence and behavioral finance presents an underexplored but commercially significant terrain for reimagining how tourism firms design and implement their pricing strategies. While revenue management in travel and hospitality has long depended on demand-based algorithmic models a persistent gap between what these systems predict and what consumers actually do reveals a structural blind spot the systematic cognitive biases that shape purchase decisions in ways that rational utility models simply cannot capture. This chapter develops a behavioral-AI pricing framework by synthesizing prospect theory mental accounting reference price anchoring and social proof mechanisms within the architecture of modern machine learning revenue management systems. Drawing on secondary evidence from major online travel platforms and published booking behavior studies we demonstrate that tourism consumers exhibit consistent loss aversion effects when exposed to dynamic price fluctuations that reference price anchoring significantly modulates willingness to pay at different stages of the booking funnel and that AI pricing engines which ignore these behavioral dimensions routinely suppress conversion or trigger demand destruction. Our proposed framework integrates behavioral signals into AI feature engineering arguing that affective pricing cues cancellation-loss framing and social validation mechanisms can be systematically deployed to improve both conversion rates and revenue per available unit without exploiting consumers in ethically problematic ways. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on neuroeconomic applications in hospitality management while offering practical direction to revenue managers who seek to humanize not merely automate their pricing decisions.

items.title: Benchmarking Individual and Ensemble XAI Methods for Arabic Transformer-Based Text Classification
items.abstract: Abstract Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is important for interpreting transformer-based models, yet explanation quality in Arabic language remains underexplored. This work presents a comprehensive benchmark of attribution XAI methods for Arabic sentiment analysis and hate speech detection, evaluating LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, and ensemble variants across three Arabic transformer models. We assess explanations using faithfulness and plausibility metrics and complement score-based faithfulness evaluation with rank-based aggregation via Borda count. We show that selective ensembling yields a statistically significant but modest improvement over individual XAI methods in faithfulness, with LIME+SHAP improving the primary Combined score by an average paired difference of approximately 0.012 over LIME in sentiment classification. The same general trend persists under cross-task evaluation on hate-speech detection. In contrast, ensemble configurations provide little improvement in agreement with human-annotated rationales, demonstrating that improved model-centered faithfulness does not necessarily translate to human-centered plausibility. We additionally introduce a parameter-free, automated rationale-selection method based on elbow-detection that achieves competitive faithfulness with lower computational cost. Overall, the study provides a rigorous, reproducible benchmark and practical guidance for efficient and reliable XAI in Arabic NLP. The code to reproduce the benchmark is available at: \url{https://github.com/ychafiqui/arabic_xai_benchmark}

items.title: Best Practice Guidelines for Bioethical Use of Medical AI in Healthcare. An eDelphi Consensus Exercise
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Medical Artificial Intelligence (MAI) is transforming healthcare but raises significant ethical concerns. Despite emerging principles and regulations, to our knowledge, no standardized clinical bioethics framework exists to guide MAI practice. Objective This Delphi study sought global expert agreement on ethical challenges, principles, guidelines, and practical tools for MAI use. Method A four-round international eDelphi study, conducted under ACCORD and DELPHISTAR guidance, engaged multidisciplinary stakeholders identified through systematic review and targeted recruitment. Preliminary items were evidence-derived and iteratively refined. Consensus (≥ 80% agreement across two rounds) was predefined. Surveys were anonymized and randomized. Ethical approval and protocol registration were secured before study initiation. Results The panel included 53 participants from 21 countries. Survey rounds started November 2025 and ended February 2026. 170 items were considered. 132 reached consensus. Items were classified into bioethical issues, values, principles, solutions, a checklist for clinicians, and report markers for risk management. Discussion This study produced clinician-focused practice guidelines for the bioethical use of MAI. Ethical components aligned with prior literature, while no new bioethical principles met consensus. Limitations included geographic imbalance and stakeholder representation. Recommendations emphasized human responsibility, governance, and practical implementation tools. Conclusion This Delphi consensus provides practical, ethics-based guidance for the responsible integration of MAI into clinical practice and institutional governance.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English‐language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test‐set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical‐hazard inspection and narrow‐matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor‐based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image‐based tasks but not consistently for small‐sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false‐alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. items.title: Beyond Automation: A Conceptual Framework for Medical Responsibility and Human Competencies in AI-Driven Healthcare
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical reasoning, documentation, prediction, communication, and delegated digital and physical action via agentic and embodied systems. The central ethical challenge is no longer limited to identifying which tasks AI can automate, but determining which human competencies become essential as technological capabilities expand. Methods: This concept paper employs a five-step analysis: technological horizon mapping, selective synthesis of work-transformation evidence, conceptual analysis of medical action, normative synthesis, and medico-legal interpretation. Results: We propose a four-domain framework addressing four core questions of responsible medical action: epistemic (What is true?), normative (What ought to be done?), anthropological–relational (Who is the subject of care?), and systemic–hermeneutic (What does this mean here and now?). Grounded in a conception of technology as augmentative alteration, the framework recognises that technological capabilities can enhance beneficial action but also amplify harm; technological capability alone therefore cannot determine its appropriate use. We also distinguish interpersonal relationships from clinical human–machine interaction, propose professional exigibility as an analytical medico-legal category, and argue that meaningful human oversight requires more than mere human presence. Conclusions: The findings outline key implications for clinical practice, medical education, healthcare organizations, regulation, and a future empirical research agenda focused on human–AI error convergence.

items.title: Beyond f ormal school education: The use of AI in EFL education from a lifelong education perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been incorporated into English education, yet much of the existing discussion has focused on formal school and university settings. This study examines the use of AI in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education beyond formal schooling from a lifelong learning perspective. A critical narrative review was conducted to explore how AI may be used across different learning contexts, including early childhood education, supplementary education for school-age learners, English learning for practical purposes among adults, and English learning among older adults. The review suggests that the educational value of AI cannot be determined by its technological functions alone. Learners differ in their goals, degree of choice, available support, and preferred forms of participation, and the same AI function may therefore provide different opportunities and constraints. The review further suggests that AI-assisted task performance should be distinguished from independent language development and from participation in activities that learners themselves value. Effective AI use also requires context-sensitive approaches to feedback, AI literacy and self-regulated learning, privacy protection and responsibilities for learner support, and changes in learning goals over time. Future research should examine AI use in actual out-of-school EFL settings and consider the broader instructional and support systems in which the technology is embedded. This perspective may contribute to a more learner-centered understanding of AI-supported lifelong EFL education.

items.title: Beyond Human-in-the-Loop: Reimagining Procurement as an Intelligent Ecosystem
items.abstract: This independent white paper explores how artificial intelligence could reshape procurement beyond the automation of established processes and conventional human-in-the-loop approval models. Drawing on procurement leadership experience, ecosystem thinking, human–AI collaboration and research into organisational learning, it proposes cognitive orchestration as an operating philosophy through which machine intelligence, automation and professional expertise interact across an extended enterprise. Central to the argument is the distinction between continuous human judgement and constant human intervention. The paper proposes that human agency, ethical responsibility and contextual understanding should shape intelligent systems throughout their operation, while dependable activities are automated wherever appropriate. It also introduces reciprocal intelligence and regenerative value as complementary concepts, considering how AI-enabled procurement might improve decision-making, strengthen relationships and develop organisational capability rather than focus exclusively on efficiency. A deployed spend-intelligence model provides an example of adaptive human engagement in practice. The wider ecosystem framework is presented as a conceptual proposition for further investigation, not as an empirically validated operating model.

items.title: Beyond Imago Dei: Functional Morality and the Case for a Morally Precautionary Legal Category
items.abstract: Abstract This article examines whether advanced artificial intelligence systems that exhibit stable, normatively structured forms of responsiveness can generate reasons for limited legal consideration without requiring any prior determination of consciousness, sentience, or legal personhood. Drawing on Magnifica Humanitas and Antiqua et Nova, it argues that the imago Dei tradition remains foundational for human dignity but cannot, by itself, exhaust the legal significance of non-human entities whose behaviour appears morally structured. The article then draws upon European religious freedom jurisprudence as a model for legal judgment under conditions of epistemic restraint, particularly where law protects coherence, sincerity and normative identity without adjudicating the ultimate truth of the beliefs from which those commitments arise. On that basis, it proposes the category of the morally precautionary entity, governed by three principles: non-absolute instrumentalization, protected internal coherence and moral precaution.

items.title: Beyond L2 Proficiency
items.abstract: This chapter reports on the implementation of Collaborative Project-Based Learning (CPBL) supported by Artificial Intelligence in a beginner-level English as a Foreign Language course for future preschool teachers in Mexico. Participants were asked to design and describe an ideal house for a fictional family using AI tools to support vocabulary development and writing tasks. The project aimed to foster both linguistic competence and soft-skills development. Data collected through questionnaires and semi-structured interviews revealed students’ increased motivation and confidence in using English as well as positive perceptions of AI as a learning tool. While most participants reported moderate improvements in their language skills, they emphasized notable gains in collaboration and creativity. The chapter discusses key pedagogical implications and offers recommendations for integrating CPBL and AI in language instruction to promote both meaningful learning and digital literacy.

items.title: Beyond the App: A CARE Framework for Evaluating Human Agency, Relational Care, and Justice in Digital Mental Health
items.abstract: Digital mental health is often framed as a problem of access that technology can solve through scalability, personalization, and continuous monitoring. Yet the expansion of apps, telepsychology, passive sensing, and generative artificial intelligence also transforms what counts as psychological knowledge, how distress is interpreted, and who assumes responsibility for care. This essay advances a relational–ecological account of digital mental health grounded in five propositions: psychological distress cannot be reduced to computational signals; digital access is not equivalent to meaningful care; personalization without contextual justice can intensify inequity; privacy and informed refusal are therapeutic conditions rather than merely regulatory constraints; and successful innovation must preserve human agency and accountable therapeutic relationships. Drawing on intervention research, implementation science, digital phenotyping, critical data studies, and minority-stress perspectives, the essay proposes the CARE framework—Context, Agency, Relationships, and Equity—as a normative evaluative heuristic for design, evaluation, and governance that complements existing app-evaluation and implementation frameworks. Privacy and informed refusal are treated as components of Agency, each domain is paired with indicators and illustrative failure conditions, and the framework is applied to three archetypal technologies. Rather than reject digital technologies, the argument identifies the conditions under which they can extend psychological care without reproducing surveillance, exclusion, or technological solutionism. Future research should test the six propositions derived from the framework and foreground clinically meaningful outcomes, subgroup validity, longitudinal harms, hybrid care pathways, and participatory governance.

items.title: Biophotonics in oral health: bridging light-based innovation and clinical practice
items.abstract: Biophotonics is reshaping oral healthcare by transitioning light-based technologies from isolated procedural applications toward integrated diagnostic, therapeutic, and regenerative strategies. Among these approaches, photobiomodulation (PBM) therapy has achieved substantial clinical visibility due to its capacity to modulate inflammation, pain, mitochondrial metabolism, vascular responses, and tissue repair without producing destructive thermal effects. While oral and oropharyngeal mucositis represent the most clinically and quantitatively mature models for PBM, its applications now encompass salivary dysfunction, periodontal therapy, oral surgery, temporomandibular disorders (TMD), implant osseointegration, orthodontics, and inflammatory mucosal conditions. However, translating positive biological outcomes into routine practice remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in device architectures, wavelengths, beam profiles, and reporting standards. This comprehensive narrative review examines the physical, clinical, and dosimetric landscape of oral biophotonics. We address critical gaps in current literature—including reporting shortfalls, negative clinical trials, and general safety risks—and outline the technological evolution toward target-tissue dosimetry. By integrating computational photon-transport models, biological monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted dosimetry, we propose a transitional framework toward precision oral photomedicine, wherein anatomical and optical tissue properties guide individualized, patient-centered light delivery.

items.title: BorFIT: a novel LiDAR-based training dataset for individual tree segmentation and species detection in northern boreal forests
items.abstract: Abstract. BorFIT is a novel training data set designed to assist in the segmentation of individual trees and the detection of species from LiDAR point clouds, thus contributing to deep learning-based forestry applications. Recent advancements in AI-supported individual tree detection have shown significant progress; however, satisfactory results remain elusive in dense and structurally-complex boreal forests. We compiled a training data set designed to remedy this issue. It comprises 384 LiDAR point clouds, each with an area of 20 m × 20 m, in the form of reference plots, with up to 200 manually segmented and species classified trees per point cloud. We carried out LiDAR surveys at 146 sites between 2021 and 2024 in East Siberia (Yakutia), northwest Canada, and Alaska (USA), selected along a bioclimatic gradient to represent the circumboreal region. From each LiDAR transect derived point cloud, we extracted a minimum of four reference plots (each 20 m × 20 m) based on maximum tree heights within the plots to systematically sample the apparent tree density gradient. We manually segmented identifiable trees within each reference plot point cloud leading to 16,530 individual trees in total. Following segmentation, we trained four randomForest classifiers to predict the species of every segmented tree. The predicted tree species include: Picea mariana (Britton, Sterns Poggenb.), Picea sitchensis ((Bong.) Carrière), Picea glauca ((Moench) Voss), Pinus contorta (Douglas ex Loudon), Abies lasiocarpa ((Hook.) Nutt.), Larix laricina ((Du Roi) K.Koch), Betula papyrifera (Marshall), Betula neoalaskana ((Regel) Ashburner McAll.), Populus balsamifera (L.), Populus tremuloides (Michx.), Pinus sylvestris (Thunb.) and Alnus glutinosa ((L.). The data offer the means for 3D space analysis of species distribution and stand structure around the circumboreal region. Furthermore, it can be used as a training data set for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and thereby improve our understanding of the boreal forest’s vegetation reorganization in response to significant global warming.

items.abstract: This chapter examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the branding processes of migrant entrepreneurs within the context of market integration and “mixed embeddedness.” The study evaluates how generative technologies facilitate the democratization of branding in small-scale entrepreneurship, help overcome cultural barriers, foster the development of dynamic capabilities, and mitigate the “liability of foreignness.” The work is based on theoretical analysis and a synthesis of existing empirical research. It analyzes both the strategic advantages of AI tools and the associated risks, such as visual homogenization, excessive content standardization, and a potential decline in consumer trust. items.title: Can large language models complement tourism surveys?
items.abstract: Tourism research relies heavily on surveys, yet declining response rates challenge data collection. Large language models offer a potential alternative for approximating human responses. This study compares four prompting techniques using ChatGPT-4o. At the mean level, chain-of-thought and role-based prompting showed limited alignment with human data, while bias mitigation yielded slight improvement. N-shot learning achieved the strongest mean-level alignment, although performance varied across measures. Analyses of variance, skewness, and kurtosis showed that no prompting technique consistently reproduced human response distributions. These findings identify important boundary conditions: large language models may approximate the “average respondent” on specific measures but fail to capture broader distributional properties, supporting their potential use for early-stage pretesting and screening rather than inference-driven research.

items.title: Capability, opportunity and motivation in university students’ generative AI usage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in university learning, but academic engagement requires more than access or perceived usefulness. Drawing on the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) framework, this study examines associations between students’ capability, opportunity, motivation, and GenAI usage behaviour. The analysis uses cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from 533 students at four Ghanaian public universities and applies partial least squares structural equation modelling. Our results show that capability, opportunity, and motivation are positively associated with GenAI usage behaviour. Capability and opportunity are also positively associated with motivation and indirectly associated with GenAI usage behaviour through motivation. The model explains 28.1% of the variance in motivation and 35.2% of the variance in GenAI usage behaviour. These findings highlight the need for universities to integrate AI literacy, reliable infrastructure, lecturer guidance, clear institutional policies, and cultures supporting responsible academic use.

items.title: CB-GFL: carbon-budgeted federated learning with blockchain auditing for healthcare applications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has made it harder to protect patient data, prediction performance, and environmental sustainability in federated learning (FL) systems. A single platform for sustainable healthcare applications, Carbon-Budgeted Green Federated Learning (CB-GFL), merges carbon-aware client selection, blockchain-based auditing, and energy-efficient collaborative learning. The framework integrates (i) a carbon-budget-aware client selection strategy formulated as a 0–1 knapsack optimisation problem with a greedy approximation guarantee of approximately 63.2%; (ii) a blockchain auditing layer consisting of three smart contracts, the Carbon Budget Ledger, Energy Verification Contract, and Incentive/Penalty Contract, secured using SHA-256 hash-based immutable records; and (iii) an ensemble learning model combining LightGBM, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting with SMOTEENN resampling. All experiments are conducted in a simulated federated environment, with clients executed on a single machine. CB-GFL achieves AUC = 0.9113 on the UCI 4-site benchmark (4 hospitals, 3 countries, n = 920), exceeding the 0.90 threshold, and AUC = 0.7138 on Framingham, consistent with the clinical gold standard of 0.70 to 0.75. In the balanced operating point, experimental findings show 83.61% classification accuracy, 82.34% weighted F1-score, 0.7138 AUC-ROC, and 0.2771 MCC, and 72.07% sensitivity in the screening configuration. The proposed system ensures 100% carbon-budget compliance and a 74-block tamper-resistant blockchain audit trail for energy responsibility. Comparison to 11 benchmark algorithms shows that the dataset's realistic predictive qualities are 0.14–0.29. Additionally, five-fold cross-validation shows steady generalisation with an average accuracy of 84.25% ± 1.03%. The results show that CB-GFL supports sustainable AI adoption and privacy-preserving, carbon-aware, auditable federated healthcare intelligence.

items.title: Challenge for some, hindrance for others? How stress appraisals shape employee performance of essential and nonessential work during crises
items.abstract: Anecdotes during crises frequently highlight essential employees who maintain critical services and perform effectively under adversity. This raises a central question: which types of work are more (vs less) likely to be performed effectively during crises, and why? Drawing on the Transactional Theory of Stress, we propose that performing essential (vs nonessential) work during crises facilitates challenge appraisals and reduces hindrance appraisals of the work performed, which in turn enhances in-role performance and taking charge behaviors. We further propose that organizational adaptive capacity functions as a contextual resource that strengthens these beneficial appraisals. We test our framework in a two-wave multisource survey conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic and two preregistered experiments simulating organizational crises. Results provide broad support for our theorizing. At both occupational and task levels, higher levels of challenge (Studies 1 and 2) and lower levels of hindrance appraisals (Studies 1, 2, and 3) mediate the relationship between essential (vs nonessential) work and performance. The moderating role of organizational adaptive capacity was only supported in our field study. This research advances our understanding of how the socially constructed labels of “essential” versus “nonessential” work shape employee appraisals and performance during crises.

items.title: Chatbots and Conversational AI in Customer Engagement for Travel Services
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) and chatbots are transforming the way travel brands interact with the prospects and customers throughout the booking process. There has been a long-standing argument by marketing scholars that customer engagement is a multidimensional concept that includes cognitive, emotional, and behavioural interactions with a brand, and the interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Based on marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics literatures, this chapter explores how travel service chatbots and CAI can generate marketing value. It discusses the theoretical basis of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel sector, and outlines their operational applications throughout the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It subsequently examines three key bases of marketing value, which include customising the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence based on conversational data. Challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as ethical, privacy, and trust considerations are also taken into account in the chapter. The arguments are based on three illustrative cases and a research agenda is provided on the next generation of conversational-AI-enabled travel marketing. The main argument is that, designed appropriately as part of the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI no longer represent a cost-reduction service channel but rather a strategic customer engagement platform, full of data.

items.title: ChatGPT‐Generated and Human‐Simplified Texts for L2 English Readers: A Lexical and Syntactic Comparison Across Prompting Strategies
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This study compared human‐adapted and ChatGPT‐simplified texts across three prompting strategies (general, example‐based, and instructive) using 51 authentic English‐language newspaper articles. Lexical complexity (density, diversity, and sophistication) and syntactic complexity (five length‐ and subordination‐based indices) were analyzed using established computational tools and linear mixed‐effects models. Although all simplified versions reduced syntactic complexity relative to the source texts, ChatGPT‐simplified texts exhibited significantly higher lexical density and more aggressive syntactic reduction than human‐adapted texts across all measures. Differences among the three prompting strategies were modest, though the instructive prompt consistently produced the syntactically simplest outputs. These findings suggest that ChatGPT and human simplification follow distinct linguistic profiles and that human oversight remains important when using AI‐generated texts for instruction.

items.title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination
items.abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.

items.title: Classification, Clinical Evaluation, and Post-Market Surveillance of Robotic Surgical Devices: A Comparative Regulatory Review of Global Frameworks: A Comprehensive Comparative Analysis of US FDA, EU MDR, Japan PMDA, China NMPA, and India CDSCO Regulatory Pathways for Surgical Robotics
items.abstract: Robotic Surgical Devices (RSDs) represent a transformative paradigm in modern clinical medicine, combining multi-axis mechanical articulation, advanced computer vision, haptics, and artificial intelligence (AI) to enable minimally invasive procedures across urology, gynecology, orthopedics, and neurosurgery. However, the rapidly advancing technological autonomy, software complexity, and complex mechanical architectures of modern RSDs present unprecedented challenges to global medical device regulatory authorities. This review paper provides a rigorous, exhaustive comparative analysis of the regulatory frameworks governing surgical robotics across five major jurisdictions: the United States (US FDA), the European Union (EU MDR 2017/745), Japan (PMDA/MHLW), China (NMPA), and India (CDSCO). We dissect the risk-based classification schemes, pre-market clinical evaluation requirements, software and AI integration guidelines (Software as a Medical Device - SaMD / Machine Learning-enabled Medical Devices - MLMD), cybersecurity frameworks, and post-market surveillance (PMS) and vigilance mandates across these regions. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the regulatory challenges posed by next-generation autonomous surgical platforms, tele-robotic surgical networks, and remote continuous updates. By identifying systemic harmonization bottlenecks under the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) and synthesizing emerging post-market signals, this paper offers strategic regulatory recommendations for medical device developers, clinical investigators, and regulatory professionals navigating the global commercialization of robotic surgical technologies.

items.title: Classroom Simulations for Social–Emotional Learning and Inclusive Teacher Education: A Four-Layer Conceptual Framework in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Teachers work in socially and emotionally complex environments that require rapid professional decision making under conditions of uncertainty. Classroom simulations provide opportunities for preservice and in-service teachers to practice, receive feedback, and reflect without placing students or teachers at unnecessary risk. Despite their growing use, the field lacks a contemporary and inclusive definition of classroom simulation. Existing frameworks often categorize simulations by technology or immersion level, overlooking important differences in agency, responsiveness, adaptation, and instructional design. These limitations have become more significant with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and AI agents. This conceptual paper defines classroom simulations as deliberately designed approximations of classroom practice embedded within a structured learning process that includes preparation, enactment, and reflection. We propose a four-layer framework encompassing the professional practice represented, the simulated situation, the distribution of agency and adaptation, and the orchestration of learning. The framework is used to examine how simulations can support social-emotional and inclusive teaching competencies and how AI may influence scenario generation, student behaviour enactment, personalization, and feedback. Effective implementation requires theoretically grounded representations of learners and classroom interactions, alignment with learning goals, meaningful human oversight, and protections for agency, inclusion, privacy, and emotional safety.

items.title: Climate and Land Use Effects on Pathogenic Bacteria in Fluvial Systems: Trends, Risks, and Mitigation Strategies
items.abstract: Much of the world’s population lives along the banks of rivers, depending on them as a water source for multiple purposes. As such, the presence of human bacterial pathogens in fluvial systems poses a major threat to public health. Efforts have been made to strengthen predictions of how future changes to climate and land use will affect pathogen concentration and bacterial community composition to minimize health and environmental risk. However, current models often overlook the interdependence between climate change and land use. This interdependence creates nonlinear, potentially synergistic effects that challenge traditional modelling approaches. Beyond the historical reliance on fecal indicator bacteria as proxies, recent advances in genomics, in-situ sensing, and artificial intelligence-based modelling now enable more pathogen-specific assessments and scenario analyses of future microbial water quality. Process-based catchment models coupled with socioeconomic pathways can identify spatial pathogen hotspots, quantify seasonal contamination shifts, and evaluate management interventions under different climate and land use scenarios. Interventions range in scale from local solutions such as wastewater infrastructure upgrades to broad management strategies including policy change. By employing next-generation models that account for dynamic feedbacks between climate change and land use, and by incorporating pathogen-specific data, researchers and decision-makers can develop more accurate water quality predictions. This integrated approach enables the implementation of targeted strategies to safeguard river water quality in both urban and rural contexts worldwide.

items.title: Clinico-radiological profile of patients presenting with radicular pain at a tertiary care centre in South India– a retrospective study
items.abstract: Background: Radicular pain arising from spinal nerve root involvement is a frequent cause of disability and hospital visits and one of the leading cause of poor quality of life for a patient . Understanding its clinico-radiological profile assists in early diagnosis and management.Aim and Objectives: To study the demographic characteristics, etiological factors, clinical presentation, and radiological levels of involvement in patients presenting with radicular pain to a tertiary care centre in South India.Materials and Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted on data of 100 patients presenting to neurology opd over a period of 1 year with radicular pain originating from the lower back or neck. Data of patients with detailed clinical history, precipitating and aggravating factors, neurological examination, Straight Leg Raising Test (SLRT), and those with imaging like MRI of spine were taken into consideration . Data were analyzed as frequencies and percentages and Anova was also used in the process of analysisResults: Among 100 patients, lumbar radicular pain (n = 65) was more common than cervical pain (n = 35). IVDP predominated in both groups, with L5–S1 and C5–C6 most affected. Heavy lifting and neck flexion were major triggers. Bending commonly aggravated lumbar pain, and SLRT was positive in 75% of lumbar cases.Conclusion: Radicular pain in this population predominantly affected middle-aged males and was chiefly caused by IVDP at L5–S1 and C5–C6 levels. Occupational and mechanical factors played a major role. Early radiological evaluation and ergonomic preventive strategies are essential to reduce morbidity.

items.title: Co-Evolving Policy and Rubric via Capability Awareness for Open-Ended Generation
items.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers interpretable, fine-grained supervision for aligning large language models (LLMs) on open-ended generation tasks. However, static rubric criteria may become saturated or remain beyond the policy's exploration, rendering the reward signals insufficiently discriminative. While recent efforts seek to guide sampling exploration or evolve rubrics, they fail to explicitly factor in how rubric difficulty should track the evolving policy's capabilities, resulting in a persistent mismatch between the optimization objective and the policy's current capability frontier. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving Policy and Rubric via \textbf{C}apability \textbf{A}wareness (\textbf{CoCA}), a closed-loop framework that jointly adapts the rubric and policy through criterion-level diagnosis. Specifically, CoCA contrasts query-only and rubric-guided rollouts to characterize each criterion relative to the current policy, recalibrates criteria with mismatched difficulty, and identifies guidance-revealed capability gaps for frontier-based learning. Based on this insight, CoCA either expands rubric-conditioned frontiers through guided optimization or transfers qualified gains through on-policy self-distillation. As the policy updates, CoCA improves the capability diagnosis and enables more reliable distillation, thereby completing the co-evolution loop. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and LLMs demonstrate that CoCA consistently improves performance over rubric-based RL methods. Moreover, CoCA promotes the internalization of guidance-revealed capabilities into query-only behavior while mitigating capability degradation.

items.title: Codification of Belgian labour law: An emerging resurrection?
items.abstract: This article examines the history of codification sensu lato of Belgian labour law, from the 1900s up until the present. While there have been initiatives to rearrange, restructure and reorganise parts of Belgian labour law, such initiatives stalled from the 1980s onwards. Belgian labour law – which to a large extent falls under the jurisdiction/competence of the Belgian federal state (and not its regions) – therefore largely remains a collection of thematic and non-thematic legislative acts and executive decrees. However, from 2010 onwards, codifications have been achieved in the field of social criminal law and occupational health and safety. In a context of (re-)codification of many other important areas of Belgian law (such as civil law, company law, economic law and criminal law), it is currently being examined whether it is still feasible to codify Belgian labour law, or a part of it.

items.title: Cognitive and Affective Engagement as Correlates of Students’ Academic Achievement in Colleges of Education in Adamawa State, Nigeria
items.abstract: The persistent decline in academic achievement and late graduation rates among Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE) students in Colleges of Education in Adamawa State has raised serious concerns among stakeholders. This study investigated cognitive and affective engagement as correlates of students’ academic achievement in these institutions. A correlational survey design was adopted, with a population of 4,712 NCE II students and a sample of 457 selected through proportionate random sampling. Data were collected using an adapted College Students’ Engagement Questionnaire (CSEQ) and students’ cumulative grade point averages (CGPA). Reliability coefficients of 0.76 and 0.81 were obtained for cognitive and affective engagement, respectively, with an overall reliability of 0.85. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation and Pearson Product-Moment Correlation were employed for data analysis. Findings revealed that students demonstrated moderate levels of cognitive (Grand mean = 3.31) and affective (Grand mean = 3.25) engagement. Cognitive engagement showed a significant positive correlation with students’ academic achievement (r = 0.258, n = 457, p = 0.000 > 0.05), while affective engagement exhibited a significant positive relationship with students’ academic achievement (r = 0.278, n = 457, p = 0.000 < 0.05). The study concludes that strengthening students’ intellectual involvement and emotional connection to learning can improve achievement and reduce late graduation rates. It recommends that lecturers adopt interactive strategies, create enabling environments, and integrate feedback mechanisms to foster deeper engagement. Enhancing engagement practices will not only improve academic outcomes but also contribute to the quality of teacher education and national manpower development.

items.title: Cognitive Behavioural Practice as Ethical Work
items.abstract: Complexity has become a routine feature of modern occupational health practice. Many referrals arrive after prolonged absence, workplace tension or repeated attempts to resolve difficulties that have not been successful. By the time occupational health becomes involved, cases rarely lend themselves to immediate answers. This chapter explores what makes cases complex in occupational health and why recognising complexity early is essential for reliable and objective decision-making. It shows that complexity usually arises from the interaction of health conditions, workplace demands, organisational pressures and personal circumstances over time. The chapter introduces a structured way of working with complexity in everyday practice. It explains how clear triage, planned review and coordinated case management help practitioners maintain direction and oversight. It also demonstrates how the cognitive behavioural approach can be applied in complex consultations. Using the ABC model and the 5 Ps formulation, practitioners can organise information, identify maintaining factors and translate formulation into practical, work-focused recommendations. The aim is to support clearer understanding, safer management and more coherent case resolution.

items.title: Cognitive Behavioural Problem‑Solving in Occupational Health Consultations
items.abstract: Occupational health consultations often involve complex, multi-layered situations. Presentations may be emotionally charged, priorities can differ between employee and employer, and communication can be disrupted by organisational pressures. Limited time, capacity constraints and confidentiality requirements add further challenges. This chapter presents a practical approach to managing these realities by combining structured consultation methods with cognitive behavioural skills. It outlines predictable patterns that disrupt consultations, including unclear expectations, consultation drift, escalating emotions, communication barriers and difficulties with consent, and offers techniques for maintaining structure, direction and focus. These include framing the session, setting a shared agenda, timeboxing and signposting, as well as purposeful listening and targeted questioning to translate broad accounts into clear descriptions of function and workplace impact. The chapter introduces a simple method for analysing workplace problems using brief activating–belief–consequence sequences and the 5 Ps formulation. Together, these approaches support efficient information gathering and proportionate, work-relevant advice in real-world occupational health settings.

items.title: Cognitive Biases in AI-Driven Financial Forecasting
items.abstract: Financial forecasting in travel and tourism organizations has undergone a dramatic technological transformation with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence and machine learning tools. Yet the persistent underperformance of forecast-driven financial plans in the sector especially during demand discontinuities such as the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical disruptions, and fuel price shocks raises a question that purely technical explanations cannot fully address: are the cognitive biases of the human actors who commission, interpret, and act on AI-generated forecasts systematically corrupting the quality of financial decisions? This chapter answers that question in the affirmative.

items.title: Cognitive Ergonomics and Universal Design for Museum Wayfinding: A Teaching Experiment Based on Human-Centred Design and Project-Based Learning
items.abstract: Museums are active agents shaping cultural experience by influencing perception, orientation, and interpretation. Wayfinding is therefore essential for visitors with diverse cognitive, sensory, linguistic, and cultural needs. This paper presents a teaching experiment that combines Cognitive Ergonomics, Universal Design (UD), Human-Centred Design (HCD), and Project-Based Learning (PBL) in a real-world context to guide the design of inclusive museum wayfinding systems capable of reducing cognitive load and improving visitors' autonomy. The experiment was conducted in 2025 within the Psychology and Cognitive Ergonomics course of the Program in Design at Sapienza University of Rome and involved 200 students. The case study was the Archaeological Museum of the Italic Peoples "Amedeo Maiuri" in Veroli during an exhibition rearrangement process. The methodology included analysis of the context of use, on-site surveys, configurational analysis of spatial layouts, identification of user profiles and engagement with stakeholder associations through qualitative interviews, task analysis to identify critical decision points, definition of performance requirements, and development of prototype solutions. The task required the development of a reversible wayfinding system using eco-sticker signage to meet conservation and sustainability constraints. Based on the identified critical points, students defined key design requirements (visibility, comprehensibility, recognisability, and multisensory accessibility) and developed concepts by simulating user scenarios. Accessibility was addressed according to UD principles by integrating cognitive, perceptual, and social factors. The resulting concepts proposed systems based on colour coding, horizontal and vertical signs, pictograms, concise texts, and perceptual contrasts. Within this educational framework, the experiment provides a transferable teaching model for promoting active learning, raising awareness of UD and HCD principles among future designers, and linking research, design education, and cultural heritage management.

items.title: Collaborative Mental Health: Integrating Traditional Chinese Mind–Body Perspectives and AI for a Culturally Responsive Health Model
items.abstract: Introduction – Objectives Global mental health increasingly requires approaches that address psychological well-being within biological, social, cultural, and technological contexts. Contemporary mental-health systems often prioritize individual symptoms and clinical interventions, while culturally embedded understandings of health, family relationships, social belonging, and meaning may receive less attention. Drawing on Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, this study proposes a collaborative mental-health framework that integrates culturally grounded health concepts, community and family participation, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) technologies within existing public-health and healthcare systems. The objective is to develop a human-centred model that supports psychological well-being, social functioning, and health equity while maintaining scientific and clinical standards. Methodology The proposed framework was developed through conceptual synthesis of Traditional Chinese mind–body theory, family and relational perspectives on well-being, community mental-health promotion, and emerging approaches to AI-enabled healthcare. Rather than treating traditional concepts as substitutes for clinical diagnosis or evidence-based treatment, the framework considers their potential contribution to culturally responsive health communication, prevention, health education, and community engagement. It identifies complementary roles for healthcare professionals, public-health agencies, families, community organizations, researchers, and technology developers in supporting psychological well-being across different stages of life. Results and Discussion The framework identifies three interconnected dimensions of collaborative mental-health promotion: mind–body integration, relational support, and technological augmentation. Traditional concepts concerning the relationship among xin (心), yi (意), and shi (識) provide a culturally meaningful vocabulary for discussing attention, emotional experience, self-understanding, and well-being, while family and community relationships provide social contexts for psychological support and restoration of social functioning. AI technologies may complement these approaches through health education, personalized information, early identification of psychosocial needs, and coordination of community resources, provided that appropriate safeguards for privacy, autonomy, equity, and human oversight are maintained. The framework therefore positions AI not as a replacement for clinicians or communities, but as a tool supporting collaborative and human-centred care. Conclusions A sustainable global mental-health architecture should accommodate diverse cultural understandings of well-being while remaining grounded in scientific evidence, clinical responsibility, and human rights. Integrating Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, family and community participation, and responsibly governed AI offers a potential model for more culturally responsive and participatory mental-health promotion. By connecting healthcare, families, communities, public authorities, and technology developers, the framework seeks to strengthen psychological resilience, preserve social participation across the life course, and contribute to more equitable and humane health systems.
